cards.front: A {{c1::domain}} is the largest classification rank.
cards.quote: A domain is the largest classification rank.

cards.front: A dichotomous key uses {{c1::paired choices}} to lead to a name or group.
cards.quote: A dichotomous key uses paired choices to lead to a name or group.

cards.front: Which single feature separates domain Eukarya from the two prokaryote domains?
cards.back: A nucleus. Eukaryotic cells have one; Bacteria and Archaea cells do not.
cards.why: RNA sequences, membrane lipids and cell walls are then used to tell Bacteria from Archaea.
cards.quote: whose cells have a nucleus (domain Eukarya), and prokaryotes, whose cells have none (Bacteria and Archaea).

cards.front: {{c1::Peptidoglycan}} is a mesh of sugars and short protein-like chains found in bacterial cell walls.
cards.back: Archaea never have it.
cards.quote: Peptidoglycan is a mesh of sugars and short protein-like chains.

cards.front: Which link attaches the fatty tails in membrane lipids of typical archaea, and which link do bacteria and eukaryotes use?
cards.back: Typical archaea use an ether link. Bacteria and eukaryotes use an ester link.
cards.quote: an ester link in bacteria and eukaryotes, an ether link in typical archaea

cards.front: Eukaryotic membrane lipids use ester links, like those of bacteria. Does that shared trait make Eukarya closer relatives of Bacteria than of Archaea?
cards.back: No. Sequence comparisons place Archaea and Eukarya closer to each other than either is to Bacteria.
cards.why: One shared trait can mislead; the tree is inferred from sequences.
cards.quote: Sequence comparisons place Archaea and Eukarya closer to each other than either is to Bacteria.

cards.front: An {{c1::autotroph}} builds food from carbon dioxide, usually using light.
cards.quote: An autotroph builds food from carbon dioxide, usually using light.

cards.front: What is a heterotroph?
cards.back: An organism that gets food from other organisms or their remains.
cards.quote: A heterotroph gets food from other organisms or their remains.

cards.front: How does a decomposer get food differently from an ingester?
cards.back: A decomposer breaks down dead material and absorbs nutrients. An ingester takes food inside its body to digest it.
cards.quote: A decomposer breaks down dead material and absorbs nutrients. An ingester takes food inside to digest it.

cards.front: A yeast is one cell with a nucleus and chitin walls, and it absorbs its food. Does being a single cell put it with the protists?
cards.back: No. It belongs with the fungi: chitin walls and absorbing food outweigh cell number.
cards.why: The key asks the fungus question before sending leftover eukaryotes to the protists.
cards.quote: The table places yeasts with the fungi: chitin walls and absorbing food outweigh cell number.

cards.front: A many-celled organism has a nucleus and chitin walls, and it digests food outside its cells and absorbs it. Which kingdom?
cards.back: Fungi. Chitin walls plus digesting food outside the cells and absorbing it match the fungus branch of the key.
cards.quote: Chitin walls, digests food outside its cells and absorbs it: fungi.
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: A many-celled organism has a nucleus, no cell walls, and takes food inside to digest it. Which kingdom?
cards.back: Animals. Many cells, no walls and ingesting food match the animal branch of the key.
cards.quote: Many cells, no walls, ingests food: animals.
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: Kelp has a nucleus, is many-celled and makes its food by photosynthesis. Does it go in the plant kingdom?
cards.back: No. In this scheme seaweeds and pond algae fail the plant test, so a many-celled alga such as kelp goes with the protists.
cards.quote: Seaweeds and pond algae fail this test.
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: {{c1::Vascular tissue}} is made of tubes that carry water; ferns have it and mosses do not.
cards.quote: Vascular tissue is made of tubes that carry water; ferns have it and mosses do not.

cards.front: Into which plant group do the loblolly pine and the flowering dogwood each fall?
cards.back: The loblolly pine is a conifer. The flowering dogwood is a flowering plant.
cards.quote: In Virginia, the loblolly pine is a conifer, and the state tree, the flowering dogwood, is a flowering plant.

cards.front: In a scientific name, the first word is the {{c1::genus}}, a group of closely related species.
cards.quote: The first word is the genus, a group of closely related species.
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: What are the formatting rules for a species name in binomial nomenclature?
cards.back: Two words: the genus, capitalized, then the specific epithet. Both words are in italics.
cards.quote: binomial nomenclature names each species with two words, the genus and the specific epithet, the genus capitalized and both words in italics
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: A student writes the loblolly pine as "pinus Taeda" in a report. What is wrong, and how is it written correctly in print?
cards.back: The genus must be capitalized and the epithet is not. Correct: Pinus taeda, in italics.
cards.quote: binomial nomenclature names each species with two words, the genus and the specific epithet, the genus capitalized and both words in italics
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: An unknown organism has a cell wall. Does that alone tell you its kingdom?
cards.back: No. Plants and fungi have walls, and so do most bacteria and many archaea, while animals have none. Wall material (cellulose, chitin, peptidoglycan) helps, but other traits are needed too.
cards.quote: Plants and fungi have walls; animals do not

cards.front: Under a classroom microscope, an unknown cell has no nucleus. Can you tell whether it is Bacteria or Archaea from appearance alone?
cards.back: No. Looks cannot decide. Change the evidence: RNA sequences or wall and membrane chemistry can separate Bacteria from Archaea.
cards.quote: When appearance stops deciding, change the evidence: RNA sequences or wall and membrane chemistry can separate Bacteria from Archaea.

cards.front: A key asks "one cell or many?" before it asks about the nucleus. Why is that a poor first split for a methane-making archaeon, E. coli and a paramecium?
cards.back: All three answer "one cell" (Methanosarcina may form clumps), so they share a branch although they come from three different domains. Asking about the nucleus first sends the paramecium to Eukarya at once, leaving only the two prokaryotes for molecular tests.
cards.quote: Asking about the nucleus first sends the paramecium to Eukarya at once and leaves only the two prokaryotes for molecular tests.
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: A classmate says yeast is a tiny plant. Design a fair test of whether yeast needs light or sugar. Name the independent variables, the dependent variable and the control.
cards.back: Independent variables: sugar (sugar water or plain water) and light (bright window or dark cupboard), giving four groups. Dependent variable: foam height or balloon size after 30 minutes. Control: plain water in the dark. Use three or more bottles per group and report the mean.
cards.quote: Independent variables: sugar (sugar water or plain water) and light (a bright window or a dark cupboard), giving four groups.

cards.front: In the yeast test, why is plain water in the dark the control?
cards.back: Neither light nor food is supplied, so it shows what the yeast does with nothing added.
cards.quote: Control: plain water in the dark, where neither light nor food is supplied.

cards.front: In a yeast test, foam forms only in the light groups, with or without sugar, and not in the dark groups. What would the results point to?
cards.back: An autotroph. Activity only with light would point to an autotroph; activity only with sugar points to a heterotroph.
cards.quote: activity only with sugar points to a heterotroph. Activity only with light would point to an autotroph.

cards.front: In 1992 DeLong searched North American coastal water for archaeal ribosomal RNA genes without growing the microbes. What did he find, and what did it show?
cards.back: Archaea in oxygen-rich surface water, with archaeal RNA up to 2% of the extracted ribosomal RNA. Archaea are not limited to harsh places.
cards.quote: In 1992 Edward DeLong searched North American coastal water for archaeal ribosomal RNA genes without growing the microbes.

cards.front: A survey near Hawaii found one archaeal group at 39% of the tiny cells detected in deep water. Why can you not say 39% of all ocean cells are archaea?
cards.back: The numbers hold only for those samples. They show that Archaea can be common outside extreme places, not how common they are everywhere.
cards.quote: These numbers hold only for those samples but show that Archaea can be common outside extreme places.

cards.front: In the 1970s ribosomal RNA showed methane-making microbes stood apart from typical bacteria, though both lack a nucleus. What does this say about treating all cells without a nucleus as one group?
cards.back: Lacking a nucleus does not make one natural group. The RNA sequences separate Archaea from Bacteria, so the nucleus question only sorts out Eukarya first and molecular evidence must sort the rest.
cards.quote: used ribosomal RNA to show that methane-making microbes stood apart from typical bacteria despite both lacking a nucleus.
cards.section: Why the course tree is a model

cards.front: A many-celled pond organism has a nucleus, cellulose walls and makes food by photosynthesis, but its embryo does not grow inside a parent. Using the key, which kingdom?
cards.back: Protists. The plant branch requires an embryo that grows inside the parent, and a many-celled alga fails it, so it falls to the leftover eukaryotes.
cards.quote: Many cells, cellulose walls, makes food by photosynthesis, and its embryo grows inside the parent: plants.
cards.section: Use the key and write the name

cards.front: Why does the course call its three-domain tree a model and not the last word?
cards.back: Many genome studies now place eukaryotes inside Archaea, so the course tree is a simplified model that scientists keep testing.
cards.quote: Many genome studies now place eukaryotes inside Archaea, so the course tree is a model, not the last word.
cards.section: Why the course tree is a model
